---
title: "Getting Started"
subtitle: "Install MLSys·im and run a first analysis in under 5 minutes."
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Prerequisites
MLSys·im assumes basic Python familiarity (variables, functions, `pip install`). No prior ML or hardware knowledge is required. Key concepts like **roofline analysis**, **memory-bound vs. compute-bound**, and **FLOP/s** are explained in context throughout the tutorials. For a full reference of terms, see the [Glossary](glossary.qmd).
:::

## Installation

MLSys·im requires Python 3.10+ and installs with pip:

```bash
pip install mlsysim
```

For development or to follow along with tutorials locally:

```bash
git clone {{< var github_repo >}}
cd cs249r_book/mlsysim
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
python -c "import mlsysim; print(mlsysim.__version__)"
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Local install recommended
Tutorials are pure Python and run in any Python 3.10+ environment. The local workflow is the supported path for the current release and matches the commands used throughout the documentation.
:::

---

## A First Analysis

For a map of `Engine`, specialized solvers, and scenarios, see
[Choosing a Python API](choosing-an-api.qmd). The example below uses the generic
single-device Roofline model.

Once MLSys·im is installed, a complete roofline analysis takes five lines. The roofline model is the foundation of ML systems performance reasoning. It determines whether a workload is limited by compute (arithmetic units) or memory (data movement). For a visual and interactive walkthrough, see [Vol I · Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_hw_acceleration_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-11)).

```{python}
#| echo: true
import mlsysim
from mlsysim import Engine

# 1. Load a model and hardware from the vetted Zoo
model    = mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
hardware = mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100

# 2. Solve -- the Engine applies the roofline model
profile = Engine.solve(model=model, hardware=hardware, batch_size=1, precision="fp16", efficiency=1.0)

# 3. Read the results
print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Throughput: {profile.throughput.to('1/s'):~.0f}")
```

The output above is produced by running the code when this page is built, so it always matches the installed version of MLSys·im.

::: {.callout-note}
## Working with units
MLSys·im uses the [Pint](https://pint.readthedocs.io/) library for physical units. All quantities carry attached units (ms, GB, TFLOP/s, etc.). Use `.to('ms')` to convert between units. Use `.magnitude` to extract the raw number for calculations or plotting.
:::

---

## Understanding the Output

`Engine.solve()` returns a `PerformanceProfile`, a structured result containing everything the roofline model can determine about the workload.

### Core fields

| Field | What it means |
|:------|:--------------|
| `bottleneck` | `'Memory'` or `'Compute'`: which resource limits performance |
| `latency` | Time to process one batch: the roofline bound plus fixed overhead |
| `throughput` | Samples per second = `batch_size / latency` |
| `latency_compute` | Time if only compute were the constraint |
| `latency_memory` | Time if only memory bandwidth were the constraint |
| `latency_overhead` | Fixed dispatch and kernel-launch time added on top of the roofline bound |
| `arithmetic_intensity` | Operations per byte, the x-axis of the roofline plot |

### Extended fields

| Field | What it means |
|:------|:--------------|
| `energy` | Estimated energy consumption (Joules) |
| `memory_footprint` | Total memory required for the workload |
| `mfu` | `Model FLOPs Utilization`, the fraction of peak compute achieved |
| `feasible` | Whether the workload fits in device memory |

::: {.callout-tip}
## The key insight
If `latency_memory > latency_compute`, the workload is **memory-bound**, and faster arithmetic units will not help.
The remedies are to increase batch size, use a more compute-dense operation (e.g., fused attention), or reduce
data movement. When the workload is **compute-bound**, parallelism and quantization pay off.

This is the same insight taught in [Vol I · Ch 5: Neural Computation](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/05_nn_computation/05_nn_computation.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_nn_computation_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-05)) and [Vol II · Ch 9: Fleet Efficiency](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/09_performance_engineering/09_performance_engineering.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_performance_engineering_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-09)).
:::

## Exploring the Zoo

MLSys·im ships with 12 typed registries (plus `Literature` and `ReferenceStats`) covering hardware, models, infrastructure, systems, agentic harnesses, and cyber-physical robotics, each carrying provenance metadata. Use tab-completion to explore.

### Hardware

Five hardware tiers spanning the deployment spectrum (plus `Hardware.Embodied` aliasing `Edge` and `Hardware.Tech` for shared technology tiers):

```python
# Cloud accelerators
mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.A100
mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H100
mlsysim.Hardware.Cloud.H200

# Workstation / desktop GPUs
mlsysim.Hardware.Workstation.DGX_Spark

# Mobile processors
mlsysim.Hardware.Mobile.iPhone15Pro
mlsysim.Hardware.Mobile.Snapdragon8Gen3

# Edge / embodied devices
mlsysim.Hardware.Edge.JetsonOrinNX

# Tiny / microcontroller targets
mlsysim.Hardware.Tiny.ESP32_S3
mlsysim.Hardware.Tiny.HimaxWE1
```

For the theory behind this hardware spectrum, see [Vol II · Ch 2: Compute Infrastructure](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/02_compute_infrastructure/02_compute_infrastructure.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_compute_infrastructure_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-02)).

### Models

Organized across seven workload families:

```python
# Language & sparse MoE models
mlsysim.Models.Language.GPT2
mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_8B
mlsysim.Models.Language.Llama3_70B

# Vision & generative vision models
mlsysim.Models.Vision.ResNet50
mlsysim.Models.Vision.MobileNetV2
mlsysim.Models.GenerativeVision.StableDiffusion_v1_5

# State-space, recommendation & embodied policy models
mlsysim.Models.StateSpace.Mamba_2_8B
mlsysim.Models.Recommendation.DLRM
mlsysim.Models.Embodied.OpenVLA_7B

# Tiny / microcontroller models
mlsysim.Models.Tiny.DS_CNN
mlsysim.Models.Tiny.WakeVision
```

### Infrastructure

Regional grids and datacenter configurations for sustainability and TCO analysis:

```{python}
#| echo: true
# Regional power grids -- carbon intensity varies by energy source
for grid in (
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Quebec,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg,
    mlsysim.Infrastructure.Grids.Poland,
):
    print(f"{grid.name:28s} ({grid.primary_source}): {grid.carbon_intensity_g_kwh:.0f} gCO2/kWh")
```

[Vol II · Ch 15: Sustainable AI](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/15_sustainable_ai/15_sustainable_ai.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_sustainable_ai_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-15)) explains why datacenter location is a first-class engineering decision.

### Systems

Cluster, node, storage, and fabric definitions for distributed analysis:

```python
# Network fabrics
mlsysim.Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR
mlsysim.Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G

# Pre-configured clusters
mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Frontier_8K
mlsysim.Systems.Clusters.Research_256
```

For full topology and cluster modeling, see [Vol II · Ch 6: Distributed Training](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/06_distributed_training/06_distributed_training.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_distributed_training_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-06)) and [Vol II · Ch 3: Network Fabrics](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/03_network_fabrics/03_network_fabrics.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_network_fabrics_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-03)).

### Domain, Scenario & Support Registries

Beyond hardware, models, infrastructure, and systems, MLSys·im exposes datasets, deployment envelopes, runnable scenarios, operational policies, agentic harnesses, cyber-physical robotics components, and cited literature anchors:

```python
# Datasets & runnable scenario bundles
mlsysim.Datasets.ImageNet
mlsysim.Scenarios.SmartDoorbell

# Deployment paradigms (latency/RAM envelopes — not chip specs)
mlsysim.Platforms.Cloud.latency_range_ms
mlsysim.Platforms.Mobile.ram

# Agentic harnesses & cyber-physical robotics registries
mlsysim.Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
mlsysim.Embodied.Quadruped.Spot
mlsysim.Sensors.Camera.Sony_IMX477
mlsysim.Actuators.HarmonicDrive.CSG_25_50

# MLOps drift & runtime overhead profiles
mlsysim.Ops.Monitoring.PsiWarnThreshold

# Cited appendix scalars & non-executable empirical anchors
mlsysim.Literature.Chinchilla.TokensPerParam
mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh
mlsysim.ReferenceStats.ClinicalImaging.RetinalPhotoSize
mlsysim.ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens

# Solver/engine defaults (not hardware specs)
mlsysim.engine.calibration.REFERENCE_MFU_SUSTAINED
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Canonical paths in Python
Always use nested registry paths in Python code (`Hardware.Cloud.H100`,
`Models.Vision.ResNet50`). The CLI still accepts short names like `Llama3_8B` and `H100`.
See [Provenance & registry paths](provenance.qmd).
:::

Complete registry listings are available in the [Zoo reference pages](zoo/index.qmd).

## Adjusting the Efficiency Parameter

The `efficiency` parameter ($\eta$) is the parameter that most affects MLSys·im
results. It represents the fraction of theoretical peak hardware performance
that is actually achieved in practice. Unoptimized single-request inference often runs near `{python} f"{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuInferenceBatch1:.0%}"` of peak, whereas well-tuned training and batched serving workloads reach `{python} f"{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuLow:.0%}–{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh:.0%}"`.

```{python}
#| echo: true
# High-efficiency forward pass (η = MfuHigh)
profile_tuned = Engine.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh
)

# Conservative forward pass (η = 0.35)
profile_conservative = Engine.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=0.35
)

# Full training step (forward + backward + optimizer, is_training=True)
profile_training = Engine.solve(
    model=model, hardware=hardware,
    batch_size=32, precision="fp16", efficiency=mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh,
    is_training=True,
)

print(f"Tuned inference (η={mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh:.2f}): {profile_tuned.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Conservative inference (η=0.35): {profile_conservative.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Full training step (is_training=True): {profile_training.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
```

Typical efficiency ranges:

| Scenario | $\eta$ range | Notes |
|:---------|:-------------|:------|
| Well-optimized training (fp16) | `{python} f"{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuLow:.2f}–{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuHigh:.2f}"` | Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed |
| Inference (fp16) | `{python} f"0.25–{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuInferenceBatched:.2f}"` | vLLM, TensorRT-LLM |
| Inference (int8) | `{python} f"0.20–{mlsysim.Literature.Training.MfuInferenceBatched:.2f}"` | Quantized serving |

See the [Accuracy & Validation](accuracy.qmd) page for guidance on choosing η
for different scenarios. The gap between theoretical peak and achieved throughput is covered in detail in [Vol II · Ch 9: Fleet Efficiency](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol2/09_performance_engineering/09_performance_engineering.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol2_performance_engineering_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol2.html#ch-09)).

## Defining Custom Models

Analyses are not limited to Zoo models. Define any model by specifying its parameters
and FLOPs:

```{python}
#| echo: true
from mlsysim import ureg
from mlsysim.models.types import TransformerWorkload

my_model = TransformerWorkload(
    name="My-Custom-LLM",
    architecture="Transformer",
    parameters=13e9 * ureg.param,
    layers=40,
    hidden_dim=5120,
    heads=40,
    kv_heads=8,
    inference_flops=2 * 13e9 * ureg.flop  # Rule of thumb: 2 FLOPs per parameter
)

profile = Engine.solve(model=my_model, hardware=hardware, batch_size=1)
print(f"Bottleneck: {profile.bottleneck}")
print(f"Latency:    {profile.latency.to('ms'):~.2f}")
print(f"Feasible:   {profile.feasible}")
```

[Vol I · Ch 10: Model Compression](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/10_model_compression/10_model_compression.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_compression_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-10)) explains why parameter count and precision together determine both the memory footprint and the arithmetic intensity of a workload.

## Companion Textbook Chapters, Labs & Slide Decks

MLSys·im is the analytical modeling engine for the [Machine Learning Systems](https://mlsysbook.ai) textbook. Every core concept connects directly to web chapters, interactive Marimo labs, and Beamer lecture decks (explore the full [Cross-Volume Textbook Map](curriculum-map.qmd) for all chapters).

| Concept in MLSys·im | Textbook Chapter · Lab · Slides | Key Topics |
|:--------------------|:--------------------------------|:-----------|
| `Engine.solve()` and the roofline model | [Vol I · Ch 11: Hardware Acceleration](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_hw_acceleration_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-11)) | Roofline model, arithmetic intensity, systolic arrays, memory wall |
| FLOPs, MACs, and compute cost | [Vol I · Ch 5: Neural Computation](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/05_nn_computation/05_nn_computation.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_nn_computation_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-05)) | Forward/backward pass cost, activation memory |
| Training memory and mixed precision | [Vol I · Ch 8: Model Training](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/08_training/08_training.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_training_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-08)) | Optimizer state memory, gradient checkpointing, mixed precision |
| Quantization and compression | [Vol I · Ch 10: Model Compression](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/10_model_compression/10_model_compression.html) ([Study sheet](https://github.com/harvard-edge/cs249r_book/releases/download/studysheets-latest/vol1_model_compression_studysheet.pdf) · [Slides](https://mlsysbook.ai/slides/vol1.html#ch-10)) | Group quantization, pruning, accuracy-memory trade-offs |
